text: A proposal can be well-written and still be unfinishable. This lesson is specifically about stress-testing scope — the single biggest reason ambitious capstones don't get completed — before you start building in Chapter 4.

This lesson covers why scope failure, not technical difficulty, is the most common reason capstones don't finish, a concrete method for estimating real time cost, the cut list technique for pre-committing to what gets dropped if time runs short, and scope-creep warning signs specific to quantum computing projects.

Three categories of time are easy to underestimate. Queue time, not compute time — running a circuit on real cloud hardware can mean minutes to hours of wait per submission, and you'll typically need several submissions, not one. Iteration count — realistic capstones take two or three passes through build, run, and analyze, not one clean pass. And write-up and presentation time — budget at least as much calendar time for this as for the experimental work itself, not an afterthought squeezed into the last day.

Before you start building, write a cut list — an explicit, ordered list of which parts of your proposal you'll drop first if time runs short, decided now while you're not under pressure. For the running GHZ example: if time is very short, drop the five-qubit extension and report the three-qubit reproduction alone; if moderately short, keep both qubit counts but reduce shot count; if time allows, add a third qubit count as a bonus. Having this written down means a time crunch becomes executing step one of a plan, not a scramble.

Watch for scope-creep patterns specific to this field: adding just one more comparison condition after jobs are already running, each one multiplying your queue-time budget; switching hardware providers mid-project, which resets your calibration-consistency assumptions; and discovering a more interesting side-question mid-experiment and quietly expanding the hypothesis to cover it, rather than noting it as legitimate future work in your final report.
Chapter 4 begins next: turning your scoped proposal into working, testable code — and why you validate every piece on a simulator before spending any real queue time on real hardware.
